USA.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: The US should proceed with the planned tariff escalation on the remaining ~$300 billion of Chinese goods and maintain pressure on the $200 billion tranche increase to 25%. This is the moment to demonstrate resolve while China's economy is under strain and domestic political support for toughness on China remains strong. Continue negotiations but from a position of demonstrated leverage.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: The threat score of +0.35 reflects a moderate but not existential threat to US interests. The $419 billion trade deficit with China remains large (BBC, 2019-05-08), and China's structural practices — forced technology transfer, IP theft, state subsidies, and market access restrictions — pose a genuine long-term threat to US tech leadership and competitiveness (USC Annenberg analysis; Fox Business). However, the US economy is performing well (Dow up ~11% YTD in 2019 per BBC), giving Washington room to absorb short-term costs. The action score of -1.0 (maximal escalation via tariffs) is justified because: (1) China has been backsliding on commitments during negotiations, as reported when talks collapsed in May 2019 (BBC: 'claims Beijing is trying to row back on a trade deal'); (2) Senator Graham and others frame this as a once-in-a-generation opportunity to change China's 'cheating ways' (Fox Business, 2019-05-12); (3) White House adviser Kudlow acknowledged 'both sides will pay' but the structural leverage favors the US since China's export-dependent economy is more vulnerable to supply chain disruption (Fox Business); (4) China's retaliation has been limited to $110 billion vs. US tariffs on $250 billion, indicating asymmetric leverage. The risk of escalation is real — IMF has cut global growth forecasts citing trade tensions (BBC) — but the cost of acquiescence to the status quo is higher, as it would entrench China's state-led model in the industries of the future (AI, cloud, robotics, green tech per USC analysis).
key_factors: $419 billion US trade deficit with China provides ongoing economic justification for pressure
China reportedly backsliding on trade deal commitments in May 2019 negotiations
US economy strong enough to absorb short-term tariff costs (Dow up 11% YTD)
China's retaliation asymmetrically limited ($110B vs $250B), indicating US leverage advantage
Structural issues (IP theft, forced tech transfer, state subsidies) threaten long-term US tech leadership
IMF cut global growth forecasts citing trade tensions — risk exists but cost of inaction is higher
Domestic political support for China toughness bipartisan (Graham, Fox Business commentary)
China's supply chain dependency creates structural vulnerability to sustained tariff pressure

CHN.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: China should announce retaliatory tariffs on the remaining ~$60 billion of US goods not yet covered, matching the US escalation on $200bn (raised to 25%) and the threatened additional $300bn. Simultaneously, signal willingness to continue negotiations but make clear that coercion will not produce concessions. Maintain strategic targeting of US agricultural and politically sensitive exports to maximize domestic US political pressure.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: The threat to China is HIGH (0.55). The US has already imposed tariffs on $250bn of Chinese goods and on May 10, 2019 raised tariffs on $200bn from 10% to 25%, with Trump threatening to extend tariffs to essentially all remaining imports (~$300bn more). This directly threatens China's export economy — the backbone of its growth model. The BBC reports the US trade deficit with China stood at $419bn, and the US is explicitly targeting China's industrial policy, IP practices, and tech ambitions (USC analysis). Fox Business reports that Senator Graham and the administration view tariffs as a tool to 'break the stranglehold China has on the supply chain,' signaling a long-term strategic containment posture, not a short-term negotiating tactic. China has already retaliated on $110bn of US goods and announced new levies on $60bn of US products. The IMF has cut global growth forecasts citing trade tensions. However, China is not yet in existential territory — the yuan has stabilized in 2019, and Chinese stock indices have recovered 12-16% YTD. The threat is serious but manageable, warranting a firm retaliatory stance rather than panic or concession. Retaliation is appropriate because: (1) conceding under tariff pressure would invite further escalation and undermine CCP legitimacy; (2) strategic retaliation on US agricultural goods targets Trump's political base in farm states; (3) China's domestic market and Belt and Road diversification provide partial insulation; (4) the US faces its own costs — Larry Kudlow acknowledged 'both sides will suffer,' and 24 states have sued Trump over tariffs, indicating domestic US political vulnerability.
key_factors: US raised tariffs on $200bn of Chinese goods from 10% to 25% on May 10, 2019
Trump threatened tariffs on additional ~$300bn of remaining Chinese imports
China already retaliated on $110bn of US goods; announced new levies on $60bn
US explicitly targeting China's tech ambitions, IP practices, and industrial policy
IMF cut global growth forecasts citing US-China trade tensions
China's stock markets recovered 12-16% YTD and yuan stabilized — not yet existential
US domestic political pressure: 24 states sued Trump over tariffs; Kudlow admitted 'both sides will pay'
Strategic retaliation on US agricultural goods targets politically sensitive US districts
